Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The former Halliburton subsidiary KBR has been charged with bribing Nigerian government officials with "tens of millions of dollars" to obtain "billions of dollars in contracts," according to court documents filed late Friday in Houston, Texas. KBR was spun off from its former parent corporation Halliburton in 2007. Justice Department lawyers filed an "information," which is generally associated with an expected plea agreement. The Justice Department had no comment on the filing, but officials familiar with the case said they expected KBR representatives to appear Wednesday in federal court in Houston. The 22-page court document outlines a complex joint venture involving KBR and the Nigeria government-owned National Petroleum Corporation charged with developing the country's oil and gas industry. The contracts involved the design and construction of a natural gas plant. The government documents say the joint venture included payments to international consultants to bribe Nigerian officials. The alleged violations of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act come after the conviction of Albert Stanley, KBR's former chief executive officer, who pleaded guilty to bribery last fall. "We are not providing comment at this time," said company spokeswoman Heather Browne in an e-mail. She referred CNN to a filing in October that cited a consortium that included KBR called TSKJ. It said, "information has been uncovered suggesting that, commencing at least 10 years ago, members of TSKJ planned payments to Nigerian officials. We have reason to believe, based on the ongoing investigations, that payments may have been made by agents of TSKJ to Nigerian officials. "The government has recently confirmed that it has evidence of such payments. The government has also recently advised Halliburton and KBR that it has evidence of payments to Nigerian officials by another agent in connection with a separate KBR-managed offshore project in Nigeria and possibly evidence of payments in connection with other projects in Nigeria." The company said that in June 2004 it terminated its relationship with Stanley, and noted his guilty plea. "By the plea, Mr. Stanley admitted that he participated in a scheme to bribe Nigerian government officials and that payments were made by agents of TSKJ to Nigerian officials in connection with the construction and expansion by TSKJ of the complex at Bonny Island," it said. KBR, which was spun off from its former parent corporation Halliburton in 2007, has been under fire for its business practices in providing logistical support to the U.S. war effort in Iraq. The Nigerian charges are separate from KBR's contracts in Iraq and Kuwait. CNN Justice Producer Terry Frieden contributed to this story.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Former Halliburton subsidiary KBR has been charged with bribing Nigerian government officials with “tens of millions of dollars” to secure “billions of dollars in contracts,” according to court documents filed late Friday in Houston, Texas.

KBR was spun off from its former parent company, Halliburton, in 2007.

Justice Department attorneys filed an “information,” a document generally associated with an anticipated plea agreement. The department declined to comment on the filing, but officials familiar with the case said they expected KBR representatives to appear Wednesday in federal court in Houston.

Government documents allege that the joint venture made payments to international consultants to bribe Nigerian officials.

The alleged violations of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act follow the conviction of Albert Stanley, KBR’s former chief executive officer, who pleaded guilty to bribery last fall.

“We are not providing comment at this time,” company spokeswoman Heather Browne said in an email.

She referred CNN to an October filing concerning a consortium called TSKJ, which included KBR. The filing stated: “Information has been uncovered suggesting that, commencing at least 10 years ago, members of TSKJ planned payments to Nigerian officials. We have reason to believe, based on the ongoing investigations, that payments may have been made by agents of TSKJ to Nigerian officials.

“The government has recently confirmed that it has evidence of such payments. The government has also recently advised Halliburton and KBR that it has evidence of payments to Nigerian officials by another agent in connection with a separate KBR-managed offshore project in Nigeria and possibly evidence of payments in connection with other projects in Nigeria.”

The company said it terminated its relationship with Stanley in June 2004 and noted his guilty plea.

“By the plea, Mr. Stanley admitted that he participated in a scheme to bribe Nigerian government officials and that payments were made by agents of TSKJ to Nigerian officials in connection with the construction and expansion by TSKJ of the complex at Bonny Island,” the company said.

KBR, which was spun off from Halliburton in 2007, has also faced criticism over its business practices while providing logistical support for the U.S. war effort in Iraq. The Nigerian charges are separate from KBR’s contracts in Iraq and Kuwait.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Court papers submitted late Friday in Houston, Texas, accuse KBR, a former Halliburton subsidiary, of paying Nigerian government officials tens of millions of dollars in bribes to secure contracts worth billions.

Halliburton separated KBR into an independent company in 2007.

Justice Department attorneys filed the case through an “information,” a type of charging document commonly used when a plea agreement is anticipated. The department declined to discuss the filing. However, people familiar with the matter said KBR representatives were expected to appear Wednesday in federal court in Houston.

The 22-page filing describes an elaborate joint venture involving KBR and the Nigerian government-owned National Petroleum Corporation, which is responsible for developing Nigeria’s oil and gas sector. The contracts covered the design and construction of a natural-gas facility.

According to the documents, the venture used payments to international consultants as a means of bribing Nigerian officials. The accusations involve possible violations of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.

The charges follow the conviction of former KBR chief executive Albert Stanley, who pleaded guilty to bribery in the fall.

KBR spokeswoman Heather Browne said by e-mail that the company was not commenting at that time. Instead, she directed CNN to an October filing concerning TSKJ, a consortium that included KBR.

That filing said evidence had emerged indicating that members of TSKJ began planning payments to Nigerian officials at least a decade earlier. It added that ongoing investigations gave the companies reason to believe TSKJ agents may have made such payments.

According to the filing, the government had recently confirmed that it possessed evidence of those transactions. Authorities had also informed Halliburton and KBR that they had evidence another agent paid Nigerian officials in connection with a separate offshore Nigerian project managed by KBR. The government may also have evidence involving payments related to additional projects in Nigeria.

The company said it ended its relationship with Stanley in June 2004 and pointed to his subsequent guilty plea. Through that plea, Stanley acknowledged participating in a plan to bribe Nigerian officials. He also admitted that TSKJ agents made payments to officials in connection with the consortium’s construction and expansion of the Bonny Island complex.

KBR has also faced criticism over its business practices while providing logistical assistance for the U.S. war operation in Iraq. The Nigerian allegations are unrelated to the company’s contracts in Iraq and Kuwait.

CNN Justice Producer Terry Frieden contributed to the report.

U.S. prosecutors charged engineering and construction company KBR Inc. with violating the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, alleging that a consortium in which the former Halliburton subsidiary participated paid Nigerian officials to obtain contracts for a multibillion-dollar liquefied-natural-gas complex.

According to court filings, KBR and three foreign partners formed a joint venture to design and build facilities on Bonny Island, Nigeria. From the mid-1990s through the early 2000s, the venture allegedly hired international consultants to help channel more than $180 million in improper payments to Nigerian government officials. Prosecutors said the payments were intended to secure and retain four engineering and construction contracts worth more than $6 billion.

The filings alleged that senior executives authorized the use of the consultants and met periodically to discuss the bribery scheme. Payments were routed through accounts outside Nigeria and disguised as legitimate consulting expenses, according to the government. KBR was accused of conspiring to violate the FCPA and of participating in efforts to conceal the true purpose of the money.

The case concerns conduct that occurred while KBR was controlled by Halliburton. Halliburton later separated KBR as an independent company. The other members of the venture were units of France’s Technip, Italy’s Snamprogetti and Japan’s JGC.

Prosecutors brought the charges through a criminal information rather than a grand-jury indictment, a procedure commonly used when a company has agreed to waive indictment and enter a negotiated plea. That suggested KBR was likely to resolve the case through a guilty plea and financial penalties, although any agreement would require court approval.

The action broadened an investigation that had already reached KBR’s former chairman and chief executive, Albert “Jack” Stanley. Stanley previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy and FCPA-related charges, admitting that he participated in the scheme and helped authorize payments to intermediaries. He also agreed to cooperate with investigators.

The KBR prosecution underscored the Justice Department’s increasing focus on corporate bribery conducted through joint ventures, consultants and offshore payment arrangements. It also demonstrated that companies can face liability under U.S. anti-corruption law when intermediaries are used to make payments on their behalf, even when the underlying projects and officials are located overseas.

counterfactuals.output:
**KBR charged in Nigerian bribery scheme tied to $6 billion in gas contracts**

**WASHINGTON** — U.S. authorities have charged engineering company KBR Inc. with participating in a decade-long scheme to bribe Nigerian officials in exchange for more than $6 billion in contracts to build liquefied natural gas facilities.

Federal prosecutors said KBR and its partners authorized roughly $180 million in payments to Nigerian officials between 1995 and 2004. The alleged bribes were intended to help a four-company consortium win engineering and construction contracts for the Bonny Island liquefied natural gas project in Nigeria’s Niger Delta.

According to court documents, the payments were routed through consultants and offshore accounts. Prosecutors said senior Nigerian officials and others were targeted in the scheme.

KBR was formerly a subsidiary of Halliburton Co. and became a separate company in 2007. The case was brought under the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which prohibits companies and individuals with U.S. ties from bribing foreign officials to obtain or retain business.

KBR agreed in 2009 to plead guilty to conspiracy and anti-bribery charges and pay a $402 million criminal fine. In a related civil action, KBR and Halliburton agreed to pay $177 million in disgorgement to settle charges brought by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Authorities described the case as one of the largest foreign-bribery prosecutions in U.S. history at the time. The investigation also led to cases against other companies and executives connected to the consortium.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the Justice Department’s Foreign Corrupt Practices Act case against former Halliburton subsidiary KBR, including Albert Stanley’s guilty plea and the TSKJ consortium.
counterfactuals.output:
The Justice Department’s case centered on a decade-long scheme to bribe Nigerian officials for contracts to build liquefied-natural-gas facilities on Bonny Island.

- **TSKJ consortium:** KBR and its predecessor, the M.W. Kellogg Company, participated in TSKJ, a four-company joint venture with France’s Technip, Italy’s Snamprogetti, and Japan’s JGC. Between 1995 and 2004, TSKJ obtained four engineering, procurement, and construction contracts worth more than **$6 billion** for Nigeria LNG’s Bonny Island project.
- **Bribery scheme:** TSKJ hired intermediaries—including UK lawyer Jeffrey Tesler and a Japanese trading company—to channel roughly **$180 million** in corrupt payments to Nigerian government and political officials. The payments were intended to secure and retain the LNG contracts and were disguised as consulting fees.
- **Albert “Jack” Stanley:** Stanley, a former chairman and CEO of KBR, pleaded guilty in September 2008 to **conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act** and **conspiring to commit mail and wire fraud**. He admitted helping authorize the Nigerian bribery arrangement and also acknowledged receiving kickbacks in connection with other KBR business. He agreed to cooperate and forfeit about **$10.8 million**; he was later sentenced to 30 months in prison.
- **KBR resolution:** In February 2009, Kellogg Brown & Root LLC pleaded guilty to one FCPA conspiracy count and four substantive anti-bribery counts. It agreed to pay a **$402 million criminal fine**, then one of the largest FCPA penalties. Parent company KBR Inc. entered a related agreement requiring enhanced compliance controls and an independent monitor.
- **Halliburton connection:** KBR had been a Halliburton subsidiary during much of the conduct but was separated from Halliburton in 2007. In a parallel SEC settlement, KBR and Halliburton jointly agreed to pay **$177 million in disgorgement**, bringing the combined criminal and civil resolution to approximately **$579 million**.

The case became a landmark FCPA prosecution because it targeted not only the U.S. contractor and its senior executive but also the foreign consortium partners and intermediaries involved in the common bribery structure.

# Houston court filing alleges KBR paid tens of millions in bribes to Nigerian officials

**Documents claim payments were used to secure multibillion-dollar contracts for a liquefied-natural-gas complex; the allegations echo an international corruption case previously resolved by KBR and Halliburton.**

**HOUSTON —** Court documents filed in Houston allege that engineering and construction company KBR paid tens of millions of dollars to Nigerian government officials and other intermediaries in connection with contracts for a major liquefied-natural-gas project.

The filing describes an extensive system of payments allegedly routed through consultants and offshore accounts to influence Nigerian officials involved in awarding contracts for the Bonny Island LNG complex. The project, one of Nigeria’s largest energy developments, generated contracts worth billions of dollars for an international consortium that included KBR.

The claims in the Houston documents are allegations and have not been proven in the proceeding. The precise legal significance of the filing will depend on the claims before the court, the evidence admitted and any response from KBR or other parties.

According to the documents, money was characterized as consulting or intermediary fees even though some of it was allegedly intended for Nigerian officials. The filing portrays the payments as part of a coordinated effort to obtain favorable treatment during contract negotiations and approval processes.

It was not immediately clear whether the documents identify every alleged recipient or establish that each proposed payment was ultimately delivered. Bribery cases frequently rely on records from intermediaries, internal communications, bank transfers and testimony from participants, all of which may be contested.

KBR did not immediately provide a response to the newly filed allegations. Nigerian authorities and officials referenced in the documents also could not immediately be reached for comment.

## Allegations tied to Bonny Island project

The alleged conduct centers on contracts for the Nigeria LNG plant on Bonny Island in the Niger Delta. The facility was developed to process Nigeria’s large natural-gas reserves for export.

KBR participated through TSKJ, a four-company venture whose name was derived from its members: Technip, Snamprogetti, Kellogg Brown & Root and JGC. The consortium obtained engineering, procurement and construction work valued at more than $6 billion.

Previous U.S. criminal and regulatory proceedings established that the consortium used agents to help arrange improper payments to Nigerian officials between the mid-1990s and 2004. Authorities said approximately $182 million in bribes was authorized or paid to secure and retain the LNG contracts.

KBR was a subsidiary of Houston-based Halliburton for much of that period before the companies separated in 2007.

The new filing should not be read as a fresh criminal conviction. Rather, it places bribery allegations into the record of the Houston case and may draw on conduct examined in earlier investigations.

## Earlier U.S. case produced major penalties

In 2009, KBR pleaded guilty in federal court to charges arising from the Nigerian bribery scheme. The company agreed to pay a $402 million criminal fine.

In a parallel Securities and Exchange Commission action, KBR and Halliburton agreed to pay $177 million in disgorgement. The combined penalties were among the largest Foreign Corrupt Practices Act resolutions at the time.

Federal prosecutors said the venture’s agents included a consultant hired to interact with senior Nigerian officials and another intermediary used to reach lower-ranking officials involved in the contracting process.

The earlier resolutions focused on violations of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which prohibits companies and individuals subject to U.S. jurisdiction from offering or paying bribes to foreign officials to obtain or retain business. The law also requires publicly traded companies to maintain accurate books and effective internal accounting controls.

Other members of the TSKJ consortium later entered their own settlements with U.S. authorities.

## Questions for the Houston court

The latest documents could raise several issues, including whether previously established conduct is relevant to the pending claims, whether additional people or entities may bear responsibility and whether any requested damages are legally recoverable.

KBR and other defendants would have an opportunity to challenge the allegations, dispute the interpretation of financial records and argue that some claims are barred by earlier settlements, statutes of limitation or other legal defenses.

The filing also renews scrutiny of the use of third-party consultants in countries where major infrastructure contracts require extensive government approval. U.S. enforcement agencies have repeatedly warned that companies cannot avoid anti-bribery liability by routing payments through agents or describing them as legitimate consulting fees.

No determination has yet been made on the newly presented allegations. The case is expected to proceed through responses from the parties, possible evidentiary disputes and further rulings by the Houston court.

counterfactuals.output:
**EXPLAINER-KBR, Nigerian officials and the Bonny Island gas bribery case**

**WASHINGTON/ABUJA —** U.S. prosecutors said former Halliburton subsidiary KBR and its partners used international consultants to channel about $182 million in bribes to Nigerian officials in exchange for contracts to build liquefied natural gas facilities on Bonny Island.

The contracts, awarded between 1995 and 2004, were worth more than $6 billion and covered several production units, or “trains,” at the Nigeria LNG complex.

KBR participated through TSKJ, a four-company consortium that also included France’s Technip, Italy’s Snamprogetti and Japan’s JGC. Nigeria LNG Ltd operated the project. Its shareholders included the state-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation, or NNPC, with a 49% stake, alongside Shell, Total and Eni interests.

According to U.S. court filings, the consortium retained British lawyer Jeffrey Tesler and Japanese trading company Marubeni Corp as consultants. Authorities said the consulting arrangements were used to route payments through overseas bank accounts and intermediary companies.

Prosecutors said roughly $132 million was paid through Tesler, principally for high-ranking Nigerian officials, while more than $50 million was routed through Marubeni for other officials. The allegations covered officials connected to the Nigerian government and entities involved in approving or administering the project.

The case did not establish that NNPC as a corporation received all the illicit funds. Rather, prosecutors described a scheme aimed at influencing Nigerian officials and decision-makers associated with the government-backed LNG development.

KBR pleaded guilty in the United States in 2009 to conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and agreed to pay a $402 million criminal fine. KBR and Halliburton also agreed to pay $177 million in disgorgement to settle related U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission proceedings.

Tesler, Marubeni and the other TSKJ partners later entered guilty pleas or settlements with U.S. authorities. The combined penalties imposed across the consortium and its intermediaries ran into more than $1 billion.

The Bonny Island case became one of the largest international bribery prosecutions under U.S. law and illustrated how ostensibly legitimate consulting contracts can be used to conceal payments to public officials.

# KBR expected to plead guilty in Nigerian bribery case

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Engineering and construction company KBR is expected to plead guilty to federal charges stemming from a scheme to bribe Nigerian officials in exchange for contracts to build a liquefied natural gas facility, according to court documents and the company’s regulatory filings.

A KBR subsidiary is expected to admit to conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and to related violations involving tens of millions of dollars in payments to Nigerian officials. Prosecutors allege the payments helped an international consortium secure contracts worth more than $6 billion for the Bonny Island natural gas project.

The anticipated agreement calls for KBR to pay a criminal fine of about $402 million. In a related civil settlement, the company and former parent Halliburton are expected to pay approximately $177 million in disgorgement to the Securities and Exchange Commission.

KBR said it had cooperated with the government’s investigation and had reached an agreement in principle to resolve the matter, subject to court and agency approval. The company has characterized the conduct as a legacy issue dating to the period before it became an independent corporation.

KBR was formerly Halliburton’s engineering and construction subsidiary. Halliburton separated KBR in 2007, completing a spinoff that left the two companies independently operated and publicly traded.

The Nigerian bribery charges are unrelated to KBR’s work for the U.S. government in Iraq and Kuwait. Those military-support and logistics contracts have been the subject of separate audits, investigations and disputes, but they are not part of the expected plea agreement in the Nigeria case.
